'''Cathleen Synge Morawetz''' (May 5, 1923 – August 8, 2017) was a Canadian [[mathematician]] who spent much of her career in the United States.<ref name="mactutor"/> Morawetz's research was mainly in the study of the [[partial differential equation]]s governing fluid flow, particularly those of mixed type occurring in transonic flow.<ref>[https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/morawetz.htm Science Lives: Cathleen Morawetz] Simons Foundation</ref> She was professor emerita at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] at the [[New York University]], where she had also served as director from 1984 to 1988.<ref name=bio/> She was president of the [[American Mathematical Society]] from 1995 to 1996.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cathleen Synge Morawetz |url=http://www.ams.org/about-us/presidents/53-morawetz |website=American Mathematical Society |access-date=January 17, 2024}}</ref> She was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1998.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199903/comm-morawetz.pdf|title=Cathleen Morawetz Receives National Medal of Science|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=46|issue=3|page=352|date=March 1999|first=Allyn|last=Jackson}}</ref>

==Childhood==
Morawetz's father, [[John Lighton Synge]], nephew of [[John Millington Synge]], was an [[Ireland|Irish]] mathematician, specializing in the geometry of [[general relativity]]. Her mother also studied mathematics for a time. Her uncle was [[Edward Hutchinson Synge]] who is credited as the inventor of the [[Near-field scanning optical microscope]] and very large astronomical telescopes, based on multiple mirrors.<ref>{{macTutor|id=Synge|title=John Lighton Synge}}</ref>

Her childhood was split between Ireland and Canada. Both her parents were supportive of her interest in mathematics and science, and it was a woman mathematician, [[Cecilia Krieger]], who had been a family friend for many years and later encouraged Morawetz to pursue a PhD in mathematics. Morawetz said her father was influential in stimulating her interest in mathematics, but he wondered whether her studying mathematics would be wise (suggesting they might fight like the [[Bernoulli family|Bernoulli brothers]]).<ref name=bio/>

==Education==
A 1945 graduate of the [[University of Toronto]], she married [[Herbert Morawetz]], a chemist, on October 28, 1945. She received her master's degree in 1946 at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Morawetz got a job at [[New York University]] where she edited ''Supersonic Flow and Shock Waves'' by [[Richard Courant]] and [[Kurt Otto Friedrichs]]. She earned her Ph.D. in 1951 at [[New York University]], with a thesis on the stability of a spherical implosion, under the supervision of [[Kurt Otto Friedrichs]].<ref name=bio>{{cite web|last=Knowles|first=Tyler|title=Cathleen Morawetz|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/morawetz.htm|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|publisher=Agnes Scott College|access-date=April 4, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=19967}}</ref> Her thesis was entitled ''Contracting Spherical Shocks Treated by a Perturbation Method''.<ref name=bio/>

==Career==
After earning her doctorate, she spent a year as a research associate at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] before returning to work as a research associate at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] at [[NYU]], for five more years. During this time she had no teaching requirements and could focus purely on research. She published work on a variety of topics in [[applied mathematics]] including [[viscosity]], [[compressible fluid]]s and [[transonic flow]]s. Even if an aircraft remains subsonic, the air flowing around the wing can reach supersonic velocity. The mix of air at supersonic and subsonic velocity creates shock waves that can slow the airplane.

Turning to the mathematics of [[transonic flow]], she showed that specially designed shockless airfoils could not, in fact, prevent shocks.  Shocks developed in response to even small perturbations, such as a gust of wind or an imperfection in a wing.<ref>Chang, Kenneth, Cathleen Morawetz, 94; used math in study of motion, New York Times, August 13, 2017, p. 18</ref> This discovery opened up the problem of developing a theory for a flow with shocks. Subsequently, the shocks she predicted mathematically now have been observed in experiments as air flows around the wing of a plane.<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor|id=Morawetz}}</ref>

In 1957, she became an assistant professor at [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences|Courant]].  At this point she began to work more closely with her colleagues publishing important joint papers with [[Peter Lax]] and [[Ralph S. Phillips|Ralph Phillips]] on the decay of solutions to the [[wave equation]] around a star shaped obstacle. She continued with important solo work on the [[wave equation]] and transonic flow around a profile until she was promoted to full professor by 1965.

At this point her research expanded to a variety of problems including papers on the [[Tricomi equation]] and the nonrelativistic [[wave equation]], including questions of decay and scattering. Her first doctoral student, [[Lesley Sibner]], was graduated in 1964. In the 1970s, she worked on questions of [[scattering theory]] and the nonlinear wave equation. She proved what is now known as the Morawetz Inequality. She died on August 8, 2017, in New York City.<ref>[http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/nytimes/obituary.aspx?page=lifestory&pid=186335200 Paid death notice] The New York Times, Aug 10, 2017</ref>

==Honors==
In 1980, Morawetz won a [[Lester R. Ford Award]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Morawetz, Cathleen S.|title=Nonlinear conservation equations|journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]|volume=86|issue=4|year=1979|pages=284–287|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/nonlinear-conservation-equations|doi=10.2307/2320747|jstor=2320747}}</ref> In 1981, she became the first woman to deliver the Gibbs Lecture of The American Mathematical Society,<ref name=bio/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Morawetz, Cathleen Synge|title=The mathematical approach to the sonic barrier|journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] |series=New Series |year=1982|volume=6|issue=2|pages=127–145|mr=640941|doi=10.1090/s0273-0979-1982-14965-5|doi-access=free}}</ref> and in 1982, presented an Invited Address at a meeting of the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]]. She received honorary degrees from Eastern Michigan University in 1980, Brown University, and Smith College in 1982, and Princeton in 1990.<ref name=bio/> In 1983 and in 1988, she was selected as a [[Noether Lecturer]]. She was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1984.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cathleen Synge Morawetz|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/cathleen-synge-morawetz|access-date=2021-12-16|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en}}</ref> She was named Outstanding Woman Scientist for 1993 by the Association for Women in Science.<ref name=bio/> In 1995, she became the second woman elected to the office of president of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name=bio/> 

In 1996, she was awarded an honorary ScD degree by [[Trinity College Dublin]], where her father JL Synge had been a student and later a faculty member.<ref>[https://www.tcd.ie/registrar/honorary-degrees/recipients.php Honorary Degree Recipients 1972–2018] Trinity College Dublin</ref> That same year, she was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Cathleen+S.+Morawetz&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-12-16|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> In 1998, she was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]]; she was the first woman to receive the medal for work in mathematics.<ref name=bio/> In 2004, she received the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize|Leroy P. Steele Prize for Lifetime Achievement]]. In 2006, she won the [[George David Birkhoff Prize in Applied Mathematics]].<ref name=bio/> In 2012, she became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society]. Retrieved 2013-02-10.</ref>

Morawetz was a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cathleen Synge Morawetz|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/cathleen-synge-morawetz-sdytqu/|access-date=2021-12-16|website=nasonline.org}}</ref> and was the first woman to belong to the Applied Mathematics Section of that organization.<ref name=bio/>

==Personal life==
Morawetz lived in [[Greenwich Village]] with her husband [[Herbert Morawetz]], a [[polymer]] chemist. They had four children, eight grandchildren, and three great grandchildren. Their children are Pegeen Rubinstein, John, Lida Jeck, and Nancy Morawetz (a professor at [[New York University School of Law]] who manages its Immigrant Rights Clinic).

Upon being honored by the National Organization for Women for successfully combining career and family, Morawetz quipped, "Maybe I became a mathematician because I was so crummy at housework." She said her current non-mathematical interests are "grandchildren and sailing."<ref name=bio/>
